title: Do This If You Want Another Year of Windows 10 Security Updates
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Michal Krakowiak/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft is offering another year of Windows 10 security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027.
                                            If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action.
                                            Other users can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you are still holding on to Windows 10, there's good news: Microsoft is offering another year of security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027. Microsoft officially ended support for the older OS last year but allowed users to join the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in order to maintain protection against viruses and hackers. ESU coverage was supposed to expire on Oct. 13, 2026, but the company is allowing enrolled Windows 10 users to receive monthly patches for another year—and it's not too late to sign up if you haven't already.  You can stay on Windows 10 through Oct. 2027If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action on your part. If you haven't, though, you can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year. To be eligible, your device must be running Windows 10 version 22H2 Home, Professional, Pro Education, or Workstations editions and have the latest Windows update installed. You must also be signed into a Microsoft account with administrator status. 
Windows users were originally able to purchase ESU coverage for $30, and Microsoft later added the option to either redeem 1,000 Microsoft Rewards points or opt into Windows Backup to get protection for free. To check your coverage or sign up, go to Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update and look for an ESU enrollment link (visible if your device is eligible). Follow the prompts to sign into your Microsoft account and choose your enrollment option. If you've already purchased an ESU license, you can apply it to up to 10 devices running Windows 10 as long as they are linked to your Microsoft account. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The ESU program does not include any new features or non-security updates, but if you want to stay on Windows 10, it's highly recommended that you enroll in the program. Microsoft has started pushing hundreds of critical security fixes each month—a handful of which have been actively exploited zero-days—so you should ensure your device stays protected for as long as possible.

title: Apple Has a Fix for Your New Apple Watch's Restart Bug
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 23, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Annice Lyn/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple just fixed an issue with the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 that caused random reboots.
                                            Many users noted their watches were unexpectedly restarting. According to MacRumors, the watch's Neural Engine appears to be timing out.
                                            Apple didn't explain what it changed to fix the issue, but watchOS 27.0.1 does include a patch. This update is exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and the Ultra 4, should be the "best" smartwatches the company has to offer. While they're minor upgrades over the Series 11 and Ultra 3, there are some key improvements, including the new S11 chip and a heart rate monitor that checks your pulse every five seconds. If you picked up one of these watches, you might have put these new upgrades to the test—that is, if your watch didn't restart on you. As reported by MacRumors, Apple's latest smartwatches appear prone to unexpected restarts. That's according to numerous posts on the site's forums, with users saying their watches abruptly show a blank screen with the Apple logo. There doesn't appear to be any particular action that triggers it: Users say their watches rebooted when recording a workout, using Siri AI, editing watch faces, or using the Maps app. Many users on this Reddit thread share similar experiences with their new watches. Some users dug deeper, pulling their Apple Watches' diagnostics at the time of rebooting. Rather than a specific function, the culprit appears to be a timeout with the Neural Engine, the hardware that processes Apple's AI features.  Users tried multiple workarounds themselves: One Redditor simply turned the watch off and on themself, and the issue never returned; others tried resetting the watch as new, but experienced rebooting again. MacRumors highlighted one case where a user received a replacement from Apple, and it, too, rebooted unexpectedly. It does appear to be an issue with the Series 12 and Ultra 4, and, luckily, Apple figured it out. 
watchOS 27.0.1 fixes unexpected reboots with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4On Wednesday, Apple unexpectedly released watchOS 27.0.1. The update has a brief changelog, with only one new addition: "This update provides bug fixes for your Apple Watch, including fixing an issue where Apple Watch may restart unexpectedly." Apple didn't clarify exactly what it changed to fix the issue, but at least the reboots should be over. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
This update is only for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 users, so don't expect to see it unless you have one of Apple's newest wearables. If you do, make sure to install it as soon as possible to avoid dealing with these unexpected restarts. To install watchOS 27.0.1, head to the Apple Watch app, then tap My Watch and go to General > Software Update.

title: I Tried Snap Specs, and They Could Be the Future of Smart Glasses
description: Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Me
body:
Snap was in the smart glasses game from the jump. The company’s original camera-equipped Spectacles debuted back in 2016, beating Meta to the market by five years. Meta’s Ray-Bans and Oakleys captured massive consumer mindshare anyway, while Snap’s smart eyewear has been less visible. With Snap Specs, though, the company is aiming to make up for lost time by delivering smart glasses that go beyond a hidden camera and voice-activated AI. At the Snapdragon 2026 Summit, I got my hands (and eyes) on a pair of Snap’s soon-to-be-released spatial-computing glasses that overlay digital graphics onto the physical world.Specs are heavy on tech but light on your face
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
There's a lot of tech packed into these black polymer frames. They're powered by two Snapdragon processors, with two full-color hi-res cameras facing outward; the tracking system supports 6DOF (six degrees of freedom) hand tracking for gesture controls; and it's all standalone, as there's no tether or wired puck handling the heavy lifting. With all that crammed into the frames, plus the battery to run it, you'd expect them to be heavy. At around 135 grams, they aren’t light, but Specs are surprisingly comfortable. The weight is distributed evenly, mainly across the frames, so for the brief time I used them, they remained ergonomically acceptable. Specs feel more like a pair of sunglasses than a bulky VR helmet. As for battery life, Snap promises four hours of mixed-use on a full charge. 
Display quality on Snap SpecsIn the interest of not alienating the people around you, Snap chose to make the lenses clear enough that your eyes can still be seen through them, but if you want to close out the world, there’s electrochromic dimming for quick transitions between clear and dark lenses. It both useful and a cool trick. Check it out:
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Stephen Johnson
                    
    
The in-glasses display is surprisingly bright. Specs' visuals are powered by a proprietary liquid crystal on silicon (LCoS) display system, and even when used in a light-filled conference room, I could still clearly see the UI and its various apps. I tested out YouTube under these borderline abusive conditions, and it streamed high-def video in 16 million colors suitably.  The display offers a 51-degree field of view. It feels like having a large floating window hovering in front of you. From there, you can use simple gestures to launch apps, watch movies, play games, and do most other tasks you can’t do from your phone. But it was the context-aware, real-world spatial computing tasks that I wanted to try—the things you can't do from a phone or PC. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
What can you actually do with a pair of Snap Specs? Snap plans to launch Specs with a full suite of both first-party and third-party apps that will do everything from improving your drawing skills to teaching you music. I tried out a golfing demo, and it made the possibilities of augmented reality glasses immediately clear. Instead of putting blindly toward a distant hole, Specs show you exactly which direction to swing the putter and adds a virtual flag to mark where the hole is. It’s anecdotal evidence, but my personal putting game improved immensely. Is it cheating? Probably, but it works. Are Specs going to be useful in the real world?A half-hour or so of testing a prototype isn’t enough time to really say whether these will be useful in a person’s real life, but I can say for sure that they’re very cool, and I’m looking forward to going more in-depth with them in the coming months as their release date approaches. Snap Specs are planned for release this fall and will retail for $2,195. (Thanks to Qualcomm for the trip to check out these glasses at Snapdragon Summit 2026)

title: Have Deletion Anxiety? The Anti-Minimalist’s Guide to Essential Mac Maintenance

body:
The following content is brought to you by Lifehacker partners. If you buy a product featured here, we may earn an affiliate commission or other compensation.
    
        
        You’re cruising through a work meeting when your boss asks you to share your screen. Your stomach drops. You have something like 15 tabs open, PDFs scattered from bezel to bezel, and four identically titled Excel spreadsheets to toggle between. Basically, your Mac’s desktop looks like your bedroom did in the eighth grade.While a messy desktop and digital clutter can be a source of anxiety for many people, it’s actually evidence of your deep work. Between an analyst keeping 15 tabs open so a model doesn't break and a strategist searching through 12 near-identical files right before a Zoom call, the clutter comes with the work.Running a standard cleanup app to achieve “desktop zero,” or digital minimalism, isn’t always the right solution. It assumes the mess is the problem, and it asks you to interrupt your workflow to fix something that isn’t broken. The fear of accidentally purging a vital draft or dataset is a pain point for anyone with years of research and work stored on their hardware.
An app like CleanMyMac by MacPaw that respects your working files and clears the system junk works the other way around: it's built to go after what's safe to remove, not the files you're actively using. MacPaw, known for user-friendly Mac software like ClearVPN and Eney, built its flagship CleanMyMac app to be a safe, quick way to tidy up your machine.
Where the slowdown actually comes fromYour open tabs aren’t the only thing slowing down your Mac; often, it’s the invisible stuff under the hood. Preview a dataset and a cache file writes itself somewhere you’ll never look. Open the same Slack PDF twice and you own two copies of it. Trial an app in March, abandon it in April, and its support files stay behind. None of it shows up on your desktop, but it’s all sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac tackles hidden hardware weight, OS health, and security threats while keeping you in control of your user assets. The app identifies potential clutter, such as old versions and duplicate downloads, without forcing you into tedious manual folder searches. It then shows you the results so you can review what it found and choose what to remove. The four spreadsheets stay put, because you’re the only one who knows which version is current.One scan, five kinds of dead weight
    
            
            
                                        Credit: MacPaw
                    
    
When you open CleanMyMac, the main tool you’ll see is called Smart Care. Click on it, and the software will automatically scan your Mac and purge invisible OS debris.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Here’s a rundown of what the app  does:Deep cleans: Utilizing Smart Selection technology, it intelligently targets and removes hidden background junk (outdated caches, temporary system files, and broken downloads) while respecting your personal work files.Scans for threats: Automatically scans for background malware and security threats to keep your online life safe.Boosts performance: Clears system memory (RAM) and tracks CPU loads to keep your Mac peppy during intense workloads.Runs updates: Flags outdated apps so you can update them, and when you want to delete them, it clears out hidden leftover files apps leave behind.Declutters storage: Deletes duplicate files (like those identical PDFs you’ve downloaded multiple times from Slack), similar photos, and forgotten large installer downloads taking up storage space.Plus, CleanMyMac’s Cloud Cleanup tool will reveal large files hogging up your cloud storage. And the app’s real-time monitors help ensure you always have space available for new files, PDFs, and research materials.Your working mess isn't the problem
    
            
            
                                        Credit: MacPaw
                    
    
A cluttered desktop, outdated files, and endless email chains aren’t the sign of a scattered brain. They’re evidence of deep, analytical work. What you don't know, and shouldn't have to, is how many gigabytes of cache files and abandoned app leftovers are sitting on your drive.CleanMyMac by MacPaw clears the background weight, so the only thing competing for your attention is the problem you're actually working on. If you're curious, there's a seven-day free trial to test it out on your own Mac.

        Buying a six-year-old refurbished MacBook in 2026 obviously isn't the right choice for some, but for this sale price of $279.99 at StackSocial, it can make sense for a student, casual home user, or anyone who needs an inexpensive secondary Mac for browsing, documents, email, streaming, and video calls. This is the Intel version rather than the better-known M1 model from later in 2020, so expectations should remain reasonable. It uses a 10th-generation Intel Core i3 processor with 8GB of RAM and Intel Iris Plus graphics, which is fine for writing in Google Docs, keeping a handful of browser tabs open, joining video calls, or watching Netflix, but it's not something I would buy for video editing, modern games, or heavier creative work.Still, the hardware has the sharp 13.3-inch Retina display, the Magic Keyboard is comfortable to type on, and Touch ID makes logging in and approving purchases easier. You also get two Thunderbolt 3 ports, USB-C charging, and a 720p webcam. Apple originally rated this model for up to 11 hours of wireless web use, although a refurbished battery that is six years old may not come close to that figure. StackSocial lists this particular machine as Grade B, so light to moderate scuffs are possible, and the included warranty lasts 30 days.

The bigger concern is how long it will stay useful. This MacBook Air can run macOS Sequoia, but it doesn't support macOS Tahoe 26, so it's already missing out on Apple’s latest major operating system update. That doesn't make it unusable, but it does limit how much life you should expect from it going forward. At $279.99, I would consider it a short-term option for a student, someone who needs a secondary laptop, or a casual user who mostly browses the web, streams video, and works with documents. It makes much less sense for anyone who wants a MacBook to keep for several more years, especially when newer Apple silicon models offer better performance and longer software support.

        Rosetta Stone Sapphire is on sale for $127.20 at StackSocial right now, giving new users a structured way to stick with language learning for a year. The appeal isn't that Rosetta Stone suddenly makes language learning easy—you still have to put in the time—but it does give you a structured way to practice without having to piece together lessons and vocabulary lists from different apps. The sessions are short, progress carries across your devices, and you can switch languages whenever you want.The way Rosetta Stone teaches is a little different from apps that rely heavily on direct translation—it uses pictures, audio, written words, and context to help you figure out meaning as you go. That said, tutoring isn't included, so this is still mainly a self-guided course rather than a replacement for regular conversation with a teacher or native speaker. For $127, it's a great sale, just be sure to redeem the code within 30 days of buying it.

title: If Your iPhone 18 Pro Is Randomly Rebooting, There's a Fix
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 28, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max users are reporting random reboot issues with their devices.
                                            These new iPhones reportedly freeze up after a failed Face ID attempt, and reboot shortly after.
                                            Apple's latest Apple Watches, the Series 12 and Ultra 4, also have reboot issues of their own.
                                            Apple released a patch for Apple Watches on Wednesday, and a patch for iPhone 18 Pro devices on Monday.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Apple released a bunch of new devices this month. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 support new health-tracking features and Siri AI, while the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max introduce the A20 chip and variable aperture for the first time on Apple's smartphones. But while all these new products are objective upgrades over their predecessors, they all have one issue in common: They keep randomly rebooting. 
What is Apple's rebooting problem?As reported by 9to5Mac, some iPhone 18 Pro users are noticing that their smartphones are freezing up after a failed Face ID scan. When this happens, you won't be able to interact with your iPhone, even if the "Try Face ID Again" button appears onscreen. Instead, after a few moments, the iPhone will reboot. It's not a catastrophic issue, but it is annoying, and it's affecting a number of users, as this Reddit thread shows. It's a similar story with the latest Apple Watches. While the Series 12 and Ultra 4 obviously don't use Face ID, users are still experiencing random reboots—emphasis on "random." Unlike the iPhone 18 Pro users, affected Apple Watch users aren't doing anything in particular when their watches reboot. They could be in the middle of a workout, chatting with Siri AI, or using the Maps app, when all of a sudden, the Apple logo appears. Some analyses showed that the Neural Engine was at fault, but Apple never confirmed the exact issue.  
Apple just released a fix for iPhone 18 Pro usersApple did find solutions to the reboot issues on all of these devices. Apple released watchOS 27.0.1 exclusively for Series 12 and Ultra 4 users on Wednesday, Sept. 23, which it says should fix random reboots going forward. Then, on Monday, Apple released iOS 27.0.1 for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. This update doesn't only fix rebooting issues, either. Apple also patched a bug that could add a color artifact on photos shoot at 2x at f/1.48 aperture, as well as a glitch that would freeze the display when opening Notification Center and Control Center at the same time. Here are the full release notes: 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max may unexpectedly restart when Face ID fails to authenticate.A color artifact may appear on photos captured at 2x under certain lighting conditions at f/1.48 on a small number of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max devices.Opening Notification Center and Control Center simultaneously may cause the touchscreen to become unresponsive.As such, don't feel the need to take your new iPhone 18 Pro to the Apple Store if your only issue is covered by one, two, or three of the above. While some Apple Store employees have swapped out affected units, this software update should be enough to take care of the issue. To update, head to Settings > General > Software Update.

title: How to Claim Your Piece of Apple's $250 Million Siri Settlement
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 21, 2026

        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple agreed to settle a lawsuit over delays with Siri AI for $250 million.
                                            If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 device between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025, you may be eligible for a share.
                                            If you're an eligible claimant, it's now time to submit your claim.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, Apple released Siri AI, the company's biggest overhaul to its smart assistant ever. If you have a compatible device running the latest updates, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, you now have access to Apple's AI-powered Siri, in addition to a number of new Apple Intelligence features. For some of us, this might seem like a welcome upgrade from a company that hasn't done as much with AI as its competitors. For others, it's a long overdue fulfillment of a promise. So overdue, in fact, that Apple may be offering a payout to make up for it.Delays in launching Siri AI triggered a lawsuitThis year's iOS updates aren't the first we've seen of Siri AI. Back in 2024, Apple advertised a new AI-powered Siri that could understand content on your screen and pull data from your various apps to inform its answers. In Apple's pre-recorded demos, for example, Siri could dive through your texts and emails to locate a family member's travel information if you asked the assistant what time that person's flight arrived. Apple said this new Siri would arrive with iOS 18 later that year, launching on compatible iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 devices. But while the company slowly rolled out Apple Intelligence features through the iOS 18 lifecycle, this new Siri was nowhere to be found.For many, this absence ranged from mildly humorous to frustrating. Some, however, found it deceptive. After all, Apple said users who bought a certain iPhone could expect it to run this supercharged Siri. You might have picked up an iPhone 16, or perhaps the previous-generation iPhone 15 Pro, assuming you could take advantage of Apple's AI-powered assistant, but those changes didn't actually arrive until last week, more than two years after Apple first announced them. Depending on your upgrade cycle, you could be on your second or third smartphone since then. 
These grievances weren't confined to grousing on the internet. The Clarkson law firm filed a suit against Apple, alleging the company misled customers with these new Siri features. While the company has not admitted wrongdoing, it did agree to a $250 million settlement to put the case aside. And if you're eligible, it is now time to claim your share of the settlement. Not all iPhone owners are eligible for a slice of this settlement. Per the terms, only customers who bought an iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model (iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e) can claim a share. What's more, there's a specific timeline during which purchases are eligible: June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you bought your iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 between these dates, you can make a claim. To start, head to the settlement's official website, then choose "File A Claim." If you have a Claim ID and PIN, you can share them here. If you don't, you can still choose to file a claim online. You can share your iPhone's serial number, though if you don't have it, you can share your Apple Account email address and the number associated with your iPhone. Claims are open from today, Sept. 21, through Dec. 21. How much will you get in the Siri settlement?While $250 million sounds like a huge payout, the final amount likely won't be: The estimated payout is $25 per claimant, though that may change depending on the number of respondents. If there are fewer claims than expected, you may receive as much as $95. As MacRumors reports, the final approval hearing is on Feb. 24 of next year, so don't expect the money any time soon.

title: I Tried Google’s New Image Editor, and It Could Replace Canva and Photoshop
description:
Google Pics has arrived.
                                                    Credit: Google
                            
        
        Google launc
body:
Google Pics has arrived.
                                                    Credit: Google
                            
        
        Google launches (and retires) apps at a rapid rate, so it's not always easy to keep track of everything that's coming and going. One of the more recent launches we've had is Google Pics, which is now available to users subscribed to Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) or Google AI Ultra ($99.99 or $199.99 a month).It sits alongside Google Docs, Slides, and Sheets in your Google Drive Workspace, and it's part Canva, part Photoshop: It does a bit of graphic design (like putting together an event poster), and a bit of image editing (like cutting unwanted objects out of your vacation photos), and if you're paying for one of those Google AI plans mentioned above, you might find Google Pics is the only image creation app you need.The web app incorporates the Nano Banana AI image generation model, and, as well as working as a standalone entity, will also pop up inside the other Google Workspace apps as and when you need it. Here's what you get and how it works.
How to use prompts with Google PicsGoogle Pics is driven primarily through text prompts, whether it's creating something new from scratch or making edits to something you've made elsewhere. From the opening screen, you can type in an image prompt just as you would with the Gemini app: Prompts for anything from photorealistic scenes to printed materials will work, and the more detail you add, the better.The Style box lets you give Google Pics a reference to work from in terms of the overall image look and feel, while clicking on the Upload, Drive, or Photos links lets you load in an existing image ready for editing. At the very top is an aspect ratio drop-down, so you can specify the dimensions of new images, though this can be edited later too.
    
            
            You can create new images or edit existing ones.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
When you make something new, you get four or five alternatives shown as thumbnails on the left, so you can click through them to find the one you want. There's also the option to generate four more pictures from your prompt, if you don't mind the extra usage. As it often is, Google is rather vague when it comes to limits: It says "higher access" will be available to users until February 2027, and that factors like image resolution affect how quickly you reach the limits.So, you could prompt Google Pics like this: "Create an A5 flyer for a 10th birthday party for Jess, happening at the village town hall at 3 p.m.-6 p.m. on Sunday, September 20. Include lots of party decorations, including balloons, streamers, and cake, and include some small print about food and drink being provided and there being plenty of on-site parking."From that prompt, Google Pics gave me a selection of suitable vibrant and fun-looking flyers I could choose from—all of them carrying that familiar AI "sheen" you've no doubt seen everywhere from restaurant menus to school event posters in recent times. It followed the brief directions and took seconds to do.
    
            
            Google Pics does graphic design and image editing.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
I also tried loading in my own photos and using Google Pics to manipulate them: You can very easily turn your photos into watercolors or comics, giving you what's effectively an unlimited box of Photoshop filters to play around with. The results aren't perfect every time, but they're usually more than good enough.This is a pretty bare-bones app though. You can undo recent edits, zoom in and out, and change the aspect ratio, but outside of the prompt box, that's just about it. You don't have any of the traditional resizing options or tools to do any drawing or touching up yourself, and there's no support for layers—so you're still going to need Photoshop and Canva around for more advanced tasks.How to edit images in Google PicsWhere Google Pics really impresses is with the editing tools, which become available after you've created something from scratch or loaded in an existing image. First of all, the app identifies parts of the image you can click on—so "church", "sky", and "mountains," for example. You can click on these specific elements to get a prompt box to make changes.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
You can also just drag a box around something on screen to bring up a prompt box: Maybe drag a box around a party balloon and add the prompt "make this blue," or select a random stranger in your family vacation photo and say "remove this person". Any edit you can describe, you can make (or at least attempt).
    
            
            You're able to select specific image elements to edit.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
As always with this kind of trickery, Google Pics doesn't know what's actually behind the people and objects it's removing, but it can make a decent AI-inspired guess based on the rest of the image and background. The results I got were mostly fine, and usually you wouldn't know an edit had been made—though bigger changes to more detailed photos, like removing buses and cars, can be difficult for Google Pics to handle.You can save up all of these various edits and apply them together, which saves quite a bit of waiting and working forwards and backwards. In the case of my birthday party flyer, I was able to add lines of text, change various colors, add in new elements, and more—and if you select blocks of text, you can edit them directly without a new prompt.Besides being useful practically, it can also be a lot of fun playing around with different edits and seeing what's possible. I got quite addicted to playing around with different photos, making changes that ranged from the large scale ("turn this into a night scene") to the small scale ("add an extra cloud here").
    
            
            Image text can be edited directly.
                                        Credit: Lifehacker
                    
    
One of the edits I made was to age a car in a scene by five years, something which I've got no idea how to do in a full image editor, and which would've probably taken me an hour or so even if I did. The end results might not be quite as precise or polished as they would be if done by a human hand, but these kinds of tools expand what's possible with quick and casual image editing.I won't be ditching Canva and Photoshop just yet, as they're still essential for different kinds of tasks, including projects where pixel-level precision is required and where various elements need to be combined together in layers—but I can also see Google Pics proving very useful, especially with its integration with the rest of Workspace.

title: This Hanging Dryer Finally Solved My Smelly Shoe Problem
body:
Meredith Dietz
                            
        
            Meredith Dietz
                
                                            Senior Staff Writer
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceMeredith is a marathon runner and stand-up comedian. As Lifehacker’s Senior Staff Writer, she covers personal fitness tech, home gym equipment, and more.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 28, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Meredith Dietz
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I'm sticking to my marathon training schedule, nor'easter be damned. Normally, that means I'd come home with soaked shoes, prop them in front of a fan, and hope they dry out overnight. And normally, that means I head out with still-damp shoes the next day. Not only is this uncomfortable, but it makes my home smell like a locker room.This weekend I had two training runs back to back in the rain, which meant my shoes had to be ready to go again almost immediately. This week's upgrade is the gadget that made it work: this Hedgehog Hanger.
The Hedgehog Hanger is my upgrade of the weekThe Hedgehog Hanger is a hanging shoe and glove dryer. You can easily hang it in a closet or wardrobe (there's a stainless steel hook), plug it in, and slide your shoes onto its arms. Instead of just warming the air, it pushes airflow through the shoes. The brand says the patented turbine technology moves humidity out of the fabric, and that a pair of shoes or gloves dries in about 15 to 30 minutes.
I really like the control it gives you. The heat is adjustable, from room temperature up through a few warm settings, including lower ones meant for leather and more sensitive materials. That matters if you don't want to blast a nice pair of shoes at full heat. There are five speed settings, and it goes up to a "tornado" mode for the fastest drying when you're in a hurry.
    
            
            The controls on the Hedgehog Dryer.
                                        Credit: Meredith Dietz
                    
    
After my first run in the rain this weekend, I hung my wet shoes on the Hedgehog and let it do its thing. By the time I was ready for the next session, they were dry, fresh, and ready to wear. I didn't have to rotate to a backup pair—or lace up soggy shoes and hope for the best.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you're a runner, hiker, or anyone who trains through bad weather, that turnaround time is the real selling point. Consistency is so much easier when wet gear isn't a reason to skip a session. That said, I do wish it were a little more affordable: If you only deal with wet shoes a few times a year, $199 is a bit steep.Still, if you train in all weather, live somewhere rainy or snowy, or have kids constantly tracking in soaked shoes and gloves, you'll get a lot of use out of this gadget. Hey, even when it's not plugged in, I'm grateful for the extra storage by my shoe rack.

title: Meta May Try to Repair Its Poor Privacy Reputation at 'Connect 2026'
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Meta
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Meta Connect 2026 kicks off on Wednesday, Sept. 23 at 4 p.m. PT (7 p.m. ET).
                                            Meta will likely show off camera-free smart glasses, which may be an attempt to improve the company's poor reputation for privacy.
                                            In addition, Meta Connect may highlight new mixed reality "glasses," as well as other AI updates from Meta.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Meta Connect 2026 is right around the corner. Like other annual tech events, such as Made by Google or Apple's fall event, Connect is Meta's chance to showcase the hardware and AI tools it plans to launch over the next year. The company may have started as a single social media platform, but it now dominates or competes in multiple tech fields, including virtual reality headsets, LLMs, and, as of late, personal AI agents, thanks to the introduction of Muse AI. Here's what I'm expecting to see at Meta Connect 2026. While the company will undoubtedly announce new AI developments this week, Meta Connect 2026 will likely also make headlines for its hardware division. Meta is well known (perhaps infamous) for its smart glasses, so it only makes sense that the company would make relevant announcements during a major tech event. But the most newsworthy moment of all might not be an "advancement," so much as a refinement. As PCMag reports, Meta is planning to announce camera-free smart glasses at Connect 2026. These glasses, codenamed "Luna," would rely on an array of six microphones rather than cameras to power AI features. That way, you could still ask Meta AI questions or give commands to Muse AI, without the need for cameras to tap into the world around you. 
Meta's most popular smart glasses currently come with embedded cameras, so why the change? It's probably not to offer users a "budget" smart glasses option. Instead, it's more likely that Meta is responding to growing backlash over its current camera-enabled smart glasses. It turns out that, as popular as these glasses are, a lot of people don't like the idea of being stealthily recorded anywhere they go. The problem was made worse by an underground industry of hackers aiming to disable the recording light on Meta smart glasses, making it even harder to know whether someone was sneakily filming you. To its credit, Meta has already responded to these "critiques." The company reportedly patched the exploit hackers were taking advantage of, so users shouldn't be able to bypass the recording light any longer: If the LED is blocked, Meta smart glasses are now supposed to disable video recording. Introducing camera-free smart glasses may be another step in that direction, but that won't change the fact that camera-embedded smart glasses are still readily accessible and easy to miss in passing. While there are steps individuals can take to protect their privacy in the face of these cameras, it's really an uphill battle. It's not just smart glasses giving Meta PR trouble. The company recently settled a massive lawsuit for nearly $18 billion, ending legal action from most of the states. The lawsuit alleged that Meta's platforms were harmful and addictive to children and teens, and in addition to financial compensation, Meta is now changing its rules for underage users on its platforms. That comes just ahead of the release of The Social Reckoning, a movie dramatizing Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen's revelations about the company in The Wall Street Journal's "The Facebook Files" investigation. Meta also recently backtracked on an Instagram feature that let anyone generate AI images from your public photos. Meta Connect 2026 could be a bit of a reset for Meta in a rather unforgiving environment. Meta could also take the opportunity to announce its long-rumored "Phoenix" mixed reality "glasses." Why the quotes? If rumors are to be believed, this device will be more of a headset than Meta's current smart glasses offerings, employing a goggles-like design, or perhaps something that looks like a "bulky pair of glasses."
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
That said, the expectation is that Phoenix will be more portable and practical than Meta Quest, the company's VR headset. Phoenix may use an external "compute puck" to handle advanced processes, which would allow the headset to be lighter than it otherwise might be. All the while, it could run HorizonOS, the same operating system Meta Quest headsets run. You might get the best of both worlds: A high-quality mixed reality experience without the need for a bulky headset.As much as Meta Connect will likely focus on hardware, AI will also probably take up much of the presentation. Expect more updates about Muse AI, the company's new AI agent that can perform tasks on your behalf—even if Meta simply takes the opportunity to promote the feature. Meta may also announce a new version of Llama, the company's flagship AI model, which hasn't been updated since April of 2025, though I haven't seen any rumors  about this specifically.   Meta Connect 2026 spans two days: Sept. 23 and Sept. 24. The keynote itself, however, is on the first day: Wednesday, Sept. 23 at 4 p.m. PT (7 p.m. ET). You should be able to access the livestream from Meta Connect's official site, though the stream isn't accessible at this time. (Meta has an option to "register" for the livestream, but it seems designed to send you an alert when the livestream is available.)

title: Why Your 'HIIT' Workouts Are Full of Empty Promises
description: High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, made headlines in the 2010s with one specific claim: that short bursts of hard work can g
body:
High-intensity interval training, or HIIT, made headlines in the 2010s with one specific claim: that short bursts of hard work can give the same aerobic benefits as longer sessions of jogging or cycling. But the HIIT videos you can stream today have very little to do with the original model, and many of them aren’t worth your time. Before we break down the difference, I want to make something clear: If you love doing videos labeled “HIIT,” and they’re part of an exercise routine that makes you genuinely happy, keep on doing them. I’m not trying to take away a thing that you love. But if you’re doing them because you feel  they’re the best way to achieve your goals, or because a trainer or influencer tells you that they’ll burn a ton of calories or build your booty, we need to sit down for a little intervention. 
What is "real" HIIT?High-intensity interval training was born as a buzzword after exercise scientists noticed that people got better at the Wingate test every time they took it. The Wingate protocol calls for people to pedal a stationary bike all-out, at a high resistance, for a pukeworthy 30 seconds. Then you get to rest for four minutes, and do it again. After further experiments, researchers figured out that the benefits they saw, including increased aerobic fitness, could be triggered by other rest/work combinations. The Tabata protocol, again done on a research-grade exercise bike (“cycle ergometer,” they call it) is 20 seconds of work and 10 seconds of rest, repeated "seven to eight times" to achieve exhaustion in the original study—or about four minutes in total. These are not workouts that people do for fun. Everyone I’ve seen recount the experience has said that it was complete agony. The scientists often note that people can rarely push themselves hard enough to replicate these protocols on their own. Workout classes and videos don't push you that hard, either. Peloton offers "Tabata" classes that ask you to do those four-minute blocks several times in the same workout, meaning you definitely didn't push yourself to exhaustion on the first one. To create a more accessible version of HIIT, Martin Gibala, one of the researchers who popularized the concept of HIIT, worked to find a version of the protocol that normal humans could do on their own, and that wouldn’t leave them so pooped they were scared to come back. His conclusion: one minute work/one minute rest was the sweet spot, and you could do it while cycling, jogging, or doing other aerobic activities. Interval workouts boomed in popularity, using a variety of work/rest intervals.Another accessible version of HIIT is the Norwegian 4x4, which uses four-minute intervals at a hard but not exhaustive effort, with three minutes' rest in between, repeated four times. This takes longer than the HIIT protocols I mention above—about 40 minutes for a complete workout—but it's been shown to be effective for cardio gains.How do newer HIIT videos compare?The term HIIT didn’t just get watered down; it mutated. When it began, HIIT was about getting more results in less time, so it built a reputation as being more efficient, maybe even superior to things like jogging. And since you don’t need a bike to do HIIT, trainers ran with that idea and started applying the term to literally anything they could think of. Bodyweight squats? Bicep curls? Sure, why not. As a result, these days HIIT means something more like “a workout video with a timer counting down in the corner.”HIIT’s popularity had been building for years when COVID hit, and from there it exploded. If you’re a trainer or influencer trying to come up with something you can easily film, you’ll probably gravitate to no-equipment home workouts. And to make them sound exciting, you’ll call them HIIT.I suspect the label “HIIT” on a bodyweight workout is supposed to translate as “good enough.” Yeah, you’re doing a few lunges in your living room, but the trainer wants you to think it’s just as good as anything you could get from a boutique studio or a full-featured gym. Maybe better. For any reason you might want to work out—burning calories 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
"HIIT" workout promises you can't trustYou can tell how far removed these workouts are from real HIIT by judging the promises they make. Are they saying they’ll improve your VO2max, which was one of the original benefits noted? They won’t—not usually. Let’s do a quick rundown: Do they burn a lot of calories? Not necessarily, but it depends on the workout. The longer the workout and the more out of breath you are, the more calories you’re burning. The truth is, 20 minutes of “HIIT” often doesn’t burn any more than 20 minutes of medium-intensity exercise like jogging. Do they burn more calories after the workout? In theory, your body keeps burning calories after a hard workout session. But there are two caveats: First, this is only significant when the workout is really intense. Second, after you do a hard workout, your body often wants to conserve calories for the rest of the day, so it all evens out while you’re lying on the couch. Even Gibala has said that afterburn is overstated.Do they help you lose weight? Diet matters more to weight loss than the amount of exercise you do, much less the specific type. Exercise can help a little bit with the “calories burned” side of the equation (as long as it doesn’t make you hungrier, which it sometimes does), but now we’re back to the reality that HIIT workouts don’t offer any special advantage in burning calories.Do they build muscle? Maybe a little, but they won’t get you the booty/arms/whatever of your dreams. You optimize muscle growth with strength training routines that ask you to lift heavy and then rest until you're recovered again—usually at least one minute, often longer. "HIIT" workouts that keep you moving the whole time, or that only have short rests, can build some muscle, but pretty soon you’ll be strong enough that the workout isn’t challenging your muscles enough to grow. You really do need to train increasingly heavy if you want to build muscle.How do I know if an HIIT video is actually good?First, ask yourself why you’re doing the video. Do you want to increase your aerobic fitness? Then evaluate whether following the video actually gets you out of breath and allows adequate rest for you to do it again. Do you want to build muscle? Then evaluate whether the video actually challenges your muscles.As I mentioned above, sometimes we do “HIIT” videos not for any specific outcome, but because it feels good to move our bodies and we like the moves in the video. This is fine and good, and it definitely counts toward the 75 to 150 minutes of exercise you should be getting weekly. But if you have specific goals, seek out the best ways to achieve them. Chances are, there’s something out there that’s better for you than yet another “HIIT” video.

schema.headline: Why Your 'HIIT' Workouts Are Full of Empty Promises

title: Your Fitness Tracker Has No Idea How Many Calories You’re Burning
body:
It would be great if Fitbits and Apple Watches were accurate, but sorry—they're not.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Beth Skwarecki

            Here are all the ways to find the right fitness wearable for you, and how to make the most of the data it can offer.
        
    
    
        
        When I test smartwatches and fitness trackers, I place a particular emphasis on accuracy. Is my running pace correct? Does the device capture the ups and downs of my heart rate? I even got a VO2max lab test to check a bunch of watches' fitness scores. But one thing I never test for accuracy is calorie burn. None of my devices come close to agreeing on the number of calories they think I'm burning, and I don't expect them to. Even scientists who study the accuracy of wearables can't answer the question in a way that's useful when you're shopping for this year's devices—but we'll get into why that is below. There was a time, before Fitbits, when nobody knew quite how many calories they were burning on a daily basis. Sure, you could calculate a rough estimate based on your body size, sex, and age. You could choose whether or not to believe the calorie readout on the cardio machines at the gym. (You shouldn't.) But the idea that a gadget on your wrist could tell you how many calories you personally burned during one particular day was revolutionary. It was also wrong.   How fitness trackers calculate calorie burnBefore I discuss how accurate fitness trackers are, let’s look at where they get their numbers. For calorie calculations, the main sources are motion and heart rate data. For motion, trackers use accelerometers to figure out when your body is moving, and by how much. If you have a watch on your wrist, and the watch swings back and forth rhythmically while sort of bouncing up and down, your gadget guesses that you must be walking. If there is quicker bouncing and your wrist makes a smaller movement, you’re probably running. 
This is the basic idea behind how trackers detect how many steps you’re taking. If you’ve paid attention to your step count, you already know some of the ways this can be inaccurate. If you’re shopping, for example, keeping your hand on the shopping cart handle may result in you not getting credit for the steps you’re taking, though this depends on the device. (For a perfect illustration of this issue, see these tests I did comparing a Garmin to an Apple Watch on a treadmill. When I rested my hands on the treadmill handle, the Apple Watch recorded 318 steps while the Garmin recorded none.)Then there’s the heart rate sensor: Since your hands don’t always move predictably during exercise, it can be easier to just tell your watch that you’ll be cycling or doing yoga or whatever. The gadget then uses your heart rate to make an educated guess about how much work your body is doing. Whatever the source of the data—heart rate, movements, or a combination—the gadget processes it through a formula to calculate how many calories it thinks you’re burning. Your age, weight, and sex may figure into this equation. Importantly, though, the fitness tracker doesn’t actually know how many calories you’re burning; instead, it’s calculating a probable number based on incomplete information. Why there's no simple test for calorie burn accuracyIf humans were robots, all built the same, all moving in predictable patterns, this formulaic approach might work. But humans are complicated, and technology often gets confused. For example, you may get different step counts if you put a device on your right versus left wrist. And the optical heart rate sensors that a lot of trackers use may be less accurate on dark skin compared to lighter skin. These problems relate to the data that the trackers gather, but calorie burn isn't a direct measurement. It's an estimate derived from doing math with the data the watch measures, and different algorithms can come up with different calorie burn numbers depending on how the algorithm is designed. The companies that make fitness trackers aren’t required to publish their algorithms or verify that their calorie counts are accurate. They can just put a device on the market, and there you are, comparing wearables on shopping sites without any information about how accurate they are, outside of the companies’ claims.Researchers are interested in fitness trackers’ accuracy, which would seem like a good thing. They want to be able to use wearables in research or recommend them for individuals and healthcare providers, and so they'll run studies comparing consumer devices to lab equipment. This sounds like a great way to answer our questions! But there’s a huge delay in actually getting that information, and it’s often published too late to be useful. By the time a researcher buys a batch of the latest model, runs a study, writes it up, submits it to a journal, and finally gets it published, several years may have gone by, and the company has moved on to the next model. That delay is why I (usually) can't use scientific studies to weigh in on the devices I write about. Here's a great example of how frustrating it can be: This review was published in 2025, and found the Series 1 was the Apple Watch that turned up the most often in the studies the authors were able to gather. The Series 9 and 10 watches were completely missing from the available data—and as a reminder, we're now up to the Series 12. With that caveat about delays, I still think it’s useful to look at the research on fitness trackers to see what themes emerge. Are any of them good at estimating your calorie burn? What studies say about fitness trackers’ accuracyTime for the bad news. A study from 2020 that looked at a variety of gadgets from Apple, Garmin, Polar, and Fitbit found that all the devices are inaccurate more often than they are accurate. The authors considered a device to be accurate if its reading was plus or minus 3% when compared to a more reliable measure of energy expenditure (that is, calorie burn) in a lab setting. Here’s how some of the top brands fared: Garmin devices underestimated calorie burn 69% of the time.Apple watches overestimated calorie burn 58% of the time.Polar devices overestimated calorie burn 69% of the time.Fitbits underestimated calorie burn 48% of the time and overestimated 39% of the time.The fact that Fitbits were roughly correct on average doesn’t mean they were useful. If sometimes your device overestimates and sometimes it underestimates, it’s not very helpful unless you know which is which. A 2018 review specifically of Fitbits found that accuracy varied greatly depending on factors like where they were worn (torso was more accurate than wrist), whether you were walking uphill, and whether you walked at a constant speed or stopped and started. The accuracy also varied by device, with the Fitbit Classic underestimating calorie burn and the Fitbit Charge usually overestimating. The devices just aren’t accurate enough to know how many calories you’re really burning
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
A 2022 study compared the Apple Watch 6, the Fitbit Sense, and the Polar Vantage V. The researchers had volunteers wear all three gadgets while sitting quietly, walking, running, cycling, and strength training. Every gadget, for every activity, was awarded a judgment of “poor accuracy,” with coefficients of variation ranging from 15% to 30%.This 2025 review of Apple Watch studies—the same one I mention above—found that calorie burn was, on average, off by about 18%. The authors mention a proposed standard from the International Electrotechnical Commission that recommends fitness trackers not be off by more than 10%. That's clearly not being met, although the researchers noted that newer models may be more accurate than earlier ones. And this 2026 study looked specifically at how accuracy relates to skin tone and to the amount of fat a person has. To the devices' credit, skin tone didn't seem to affect calorie counts very much, but adiposity (fat content) did. The higher a volunteer's body fat percentage was, the more inaccurate their calorie burn result. The Garmin Forerunner 955 and Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 seriously overestimated calories; the Apple Watch Series 8 also overestimated but not as much; and the Fitbit Sense 2 underestimated when it wasn't producing wild outliers. The authors concluded that all devices "substantially misestimate" calorie burn during exercise.To get a sense of these percentages, let's say your true calorie burn is 2,000 calories per day. A device that's off by 15%—on the low end of what these studies found—might report that you burned 1,700 calories, or that you burned 2,300. If you're using your device to figure out how much to eat, you could be way off in meeting your calorie goals. If these devices are all inaccurate, how can you know how many calories you're burning?It’s probably most useful if you think of your calorie burn as a number you cannot measure directly. Treat it as a black box: I burn some unknowable number of calories; now what? The only common reason you would need an accurate estimate of calorie burn is if you are trying to figure out how much food you need to eat. If you want to lose weight, you want to eat less than you burn; if you want to gain weight, you want the reverse; and if you’re trying to maintain your weight, you want to eat roughly the same as what you burn. But think about it this way: you don't actually need to know your calorie burn if you have the other two terms in the equation—your calorie intake and your weight. It's considered more accurate to adjust how much to eat based directly on your weight, rather than using calorie burn estimates as a middleman. Let’s say you’re training for a marathon and you want to make sure you fuel yourself appropriately. Well, if you’re under-eating, you’ll start to lose weight. When you start to see the scale trending downward, that’s your signal to add a few hundred calories to your diet. If, after that adjustment, your weight stays steady, then you know you’re eating the right amount. As you increase your training (or if you take time off to rest a sprained ankle), you can make more adjustments as you go. I have a post here detailing how to make these adjustments with the help of either a paid app, a group of free apps, or a DIY spreadsheet. If you’ve been using a fitness tracker instead, and it’s working for you, feel free to keep using it. But if the tracker ever stops giving you the results you want, you can safely leave it out of the equation.
